title: New lump in the unaffected breast

header.contentArea: Clinical breast examination and differential diagnosis of a new lump
guidelineVersions: NICE NG12: Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (Published June 2015; last updated May 2025)
NICE NG101: Early and locally advanced breast cancer (Published 18 July 2018; last updated 14 April 2025)

related.why: The core examination technique now applied to a new site
The contrasting history-taking approach to a lump near the original site

brief.scenario: Ms Linford, 45, now on annual surveillance for her unaffected side, reports a new lump in that breast, unrelated to her previous cancer site.
brief.task: Examine the lump and present your findings and differential diagnosis. You will be stopped at 6 minutes.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Examine systematically, characterise the lump fully, and generate a genuine differential rather than jumping to either reassurance or alarm.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Anchoring on malignancy because of her history, or dismissing the lump as benign because it's a different breast to her original cancer.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Before I examine, can I ask a few quick questions about the lump?"

flow: Brief history: onset, change, pain, cyclical variation
At 6 minutes: present findings and differential

grid.label: Brief focused history
grid.fail: Examines without any history of onset, change or associated symptoms.
grid.pass: Establishes onset, whether it varies with her cycle, and whether it has changed in size.
grid.high: Asks specifically whether this feels the same as, or different from, lumps she has had assessed before, given her cancer history.

grid.label: Inspection
grid.fail: Does not inspect both breasts or check for skin/nipple changes.
grid.pass: Inspects both breasts systematically for symmetry, skin changes and nipple changes.
grid.high: Also inspects with arms raised and hands on hips to bring out any subtle skin tethering.

grid.label: Characterising the lump
grid.fail: Palpates without describing size, shape, consistency, mobility or borders.
grid.pass: Systematically describes the lump's size, shape, consistency, mobility and border definition.
grid.high: Correlates findings with likely differentials as they go (e.g. smooth, mobile and well-defined suggesting a fibroadenoma) rather than describing features in isolation.

grid.label: Regional examination
grid.fail: Does not examine the axilla or other nodal areas.
grid.pass: Examines the axilla and supraclavicular fossa for lymphadenopathy.
grid.high: Explains why this step matters regardless of how benign the breast lump itself appears.

grid.label: Presentation of findings
grid.fail: Gives either a confident diagnosis or excessive alarm without justification.
grid.pass: Presents findings clearly and gives a sensible differential, including benign causes such as fibroadenoma or cyst, without dismissing the need for further assessment.
grid.high: Explicitly explains why her cancer history changes the threshold for further assessment even if the lump has benign features.

grid.label: Next steps
grid.pass: Recommends triple assessment (imaging plus or minus biopsy) to confirm the nature of the lump, given her cancer history.
grid.high: Explains this is about confirming the diagnosis with appropriate urgency, not because the examination findings themselves are especially concerning.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Before I examine, a few quick questions - when did this start, has it changed, does it vary with your cycle, and does it feel similar to or different from lumps you've had checked before?

high.speaker: patient

high.speaker: candidate

high.speaker: candidate

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A smooth, mobile, well-defined lump, distinct in character from her original cancer, with no lymphadenopathy - most consistent with a benign cause such as fibroadenoma. However, given her personal history, I wouldn't reassure her based on examination alone; this still needs formal imaging and likely biopsy, with an appropriately urgent, though not panicked, timeframe.

high.text: Arrange urgent triple assessment - imaging and biopsy if indicated - explaining to her that this is standard practice given her history, not because the examination itself is especially worrying.

failures.move: Assuming malignancy purely because of her cancer history, regardless of examination findings.
failures.consequence: Causes disproportionate distress and risks framing every future finding through the lens of her past diagnosis rather than what is actually found.

failures.move: Omitting nodal examination because the breast lump seems benign.
failures.consequence: A complete breast assessment always includes regional nodes, regardless of how reassuring the primary lump appears.

failures.move: Jumping to a major surgical plan (e.g. mastectomy) before any imaging or biopsy confirms the diagnosis.
failures.consequence: Proposes a drastic, irreversible intervention without the diagnostic basis to justify it.

failures.move: Fails to inspect the breasts at all before palpating.
failures.consequence: Misses skin or nipple changes that could indicate a more concerning pathology.

failures.move: Palpates the lump without describing its size, shape, consistency, mobility or borders.
failures.consequence: Gives no basis for a genuine differential diagnosis, however the case then unfolds.

recovery.when: You assumed malignancy without examination-based justification
recovery.line: Let me be more precise about what the examination actually shows before drawing conclusions.
I should also check the nodal areas as part of a complete assessment.

knowledge.fact: A smooth, mobile, well-defined, rubbery lump is a classical clinical description of a fibroadenoma, though examination alone cannot exclude malignancy.
A personal history of breast cancer lowers the threshold for formal triple assessment of any new lump, regardless of how benign it appears clinically.
A complete breast examination always includes assessment of the axillary and supraclavicular lymph nodes, regardless of the character of the primary finding.

recall.think: Describe what's found, not what her history suggests; nodes matter regardless of feel; confirm, don't assume.
recall.say: "I wouldn't reassure her based on examination alone."
do: Take a brief history, comparing to previous lumps
Characterise the lump; examine nodes regardless of feel
Recommend triple assessment, not reassurance or alarm

numbers.meaning: maximum wait for suspected cancer referral, given her cancer history

recall.trap: Anchoring on malignancy from her history, rather than letting examination findings speak for themselves.
recall.finish: A clear differential grounded in examination, with triple assessment arranged given her history.

partner.opening: Please examine this patient's new breast lump. I'll stop you at 6 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Rachel Linford, 45, on routine surveillance, with a new lump in your previously unaffected breast, noticed a month ago, unchanged, not cycle-related. It feels different (softer, more mobile) from your original cancer, though you're anxious given your history.

reveals.trigger: Asks about onset, change and comparison to previous lumps
reveals.finding: One month, unchanged, non-cyclical, feels softer and more mobile than the original cancer.
Smooth, well-defined, mobile, rubbery lump, roughly 2 cm.
Say: "Please stop there and present your findings."

push.question: Is this the cancer coming back?
push.expect: Explain the findings are more consistent with a benign cause, while being honest that formal assessment is still needed given her history.

push.question: What happens next?
push.expect: Arrange triple assessment, framed as standard practice given her history rather than a sign of high suspicion.

curveballs.prompt: There's also been some dimpling of the skin over it that I only just noticed.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Take this seriously as a potential red-flag feature, examine it specifically, and factor it into a more cautious differential and more urgent assessment.

curveballs.prompt: Can you just tell me it's nothing so I can stop worrying?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Avoid false reassurance; explain honestly that the features seen are reassuring but that confirmation requires proper assessment, which will be arranged promptly.
